new_statements.quote: El idioma yagua es tonal. Es decir que cada sílaba lleva uno o dos niveles de tono que contribuyen al carácter léxico de las palabras y pueden diferenciar entre el significado de algunas palabras que son iguales en otros aspectos fonológicos, por ejemplo, váñu "majás" y vañú "vámonos". Hay sólo dos tonos diferenciados, alto (escrito con el acento ortográfico) y bajo, de tal manera que vienen a ser como un acento tonal. [...] Las palabras yaguas cambian el tono según el contexto. Por ejemplo, se dice né saatú "él no toma" pero né saaturúy "él no quiere tomar". El acento en la raíz del verbo "tomar" (jatú) se pierde ante el sufijo rúy, que indica deseo de hacer.
new_statements.translation: The Yagua language is tonal. That is, each syllable carries one or two levels of tone which contribute to the lexical character of words and can distinguish the meaning of some words that are identical in other phonological respects, for example váñu 'paca' and vañú 'let's go'. There are only two distinct tones, high (written with the orthographic accent) and low, so that they amount to something like a pitch accent. [...] Yagua words change their tone according to context. For example one says né saatú 'he does not drink' but né saaturúy 'he does not want to drink'. The accent on the root of the verb 'drink' (jatú) is lost before the suffix rúy, which indicates desire to do.
new_statements.citation: Powlison, Paul S. 1995. Diccionario Yagua-Castellano (Serie Lingüística Peruana 35). Lima: Ministerio de Educación / Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 771 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2, final stress = fixed final stress) records Yagua as a word-stress language with final stress. Powlison instead describes a two-tone system with lexical contrast, likened to a pitch accent, and gives no word-stress rule and no fixed final prominence: the high tone is lexically distributed (váñu vs. vañú; satíy vs. satíiy; sajáy vs. sajááy on p. 27) and moves with morphology. Different prosodic type, so 'contradicts'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yagua is described as a tone language with two tones, high (written with the acute accent) and low; tone is lexically contrastive (minimal pair váñu/vañú), a long vowel may carry a high-low or low-high sequence, and the high tone is likened to a pitch accent ('como un acento tonal'). Tone shifts with morphological context (root high tone lost before the desiderative -rúy) and with emphasis. No word-stress placement rule is stated anywhere in the grammatical notes; 'acento' throughout means the written high-tone mark.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 27: high tone of a verb root is lost before the suffix -rúy; tone can change with emphasis (sadáátya vs. sadaatyájuú). p. 28: the consonants d, j, n can carry tone when they are syllable nuclei ('las consonantes d, j, n también pueden llevar el tono cuando funcionan como núcleo de una sílaba que no tiene vocal').
new_statements.identity_note: Powlison 1995 is an ILV dictionary prepared for one dialect ('En el dialecto para el cual se preparó este material', Apuntes gramaticales p. 26, dialect not named there); D. Payne 1985 argues for a six-vowel analysis 'at least in some dialects' (p. 30). Both describe Yagua proper (yad), not Peba or Yameo. Peña 2009 (held by the project from our earlier reading, not in this works list) uses the accent mark for high tone in Yagua but for stress in Yameo, a different Peba-Yaguan language.

new_statements.quote: There are two phonemic tones, but syllables are lexically marked for three types of tone features. Syllables which have an inherent high tone are marked with the accute accent. [...] Syllables with inherent low tone are marked with the grave accent. These are syllables which must always have a low tone, and which may cause placement of a high tone on a preceding syllable. [...] Syllables which do not have inherent tone assignment are not marked, even when they receive (predictable) surface high tone in certain contexts. [...] The intonational pivot occurs on the last inherent high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase. The pivot is marked by high tone. If the pivot is the last syllable of the phrase, the intonation of the phrase goes up, and stays up.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records fixed final word stress (StressTyp2). Payne 1985 describes lexical tone (two phonemic tones, three lexical marking classes) and a phrase-level intonational pivot, not word stress. The pivot is the likely origin of a 'final' coding, but it is a property of the intonational phrase, is realized as high tone, and does not fall on the last syllable when inherent-low syllables follow; it is therefore not word-final stress. Different type and domain, so 'contradicts'; the p. 43 remark that free pronouns carry stress is compatible with stress existing as a phonetic property but gives no placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two phonemic tones (high, low) with three lexical classes of syllable: inherent high (acute), inherent low (grave), and unmarked (surface tone predictable from position relative to the intonational pivot and to inherent-low syllables). The only prominence rule is phrase-level: an 'intonational pivot' marked by high tone falls on the last inherent-high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase; if inherent-low syllables follow, the phrase melody falls after the pivot. The one explicit mention of stress is that free pronouns carry stress whereas the segmentally identical Set II clitics do not (p. 43). No word-stress placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 31: a phrase-final high tone following another high tone may be phonetically mid; a high tone may be realized as a high-low glide over a short vowel plus a following sonorant when another high tone follows. p. 43: 'Both bound and free forms are isomorphic with free pronouns except that the latter carry stress.' §2.4 (ex. 133-136): paratactic phrases may be integrated into one phonological phrase with no pivot before them, or treated as non-final with a pause but no pivot.

readall_conflicts: The two sources actually read (Powlison 1995; D. Payne 1985) agree with each other: Yagua has two phonemic tones, high and low, with lexical contrast (Powlison: váñu 'paca' vs. vañú 'let's go'; Payne: three lexical classes of syllable, inherent high / inherent low / unmarked). Powlison likens the system to a pitch accent; Payne adds a phrase-level intonational pivot realized as high tone on the last inherent-high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase, and remarks that free pronouns carry stress while the homophonous Set II clitics do not. Neither gives a word-stress placement rule. Both therefore disagree with the catalog's StressTyp2 record, which codes Yagua as fixed final word stress (final stress): the only final-ish prominence in the sources is Payne's intonational pivot, which is a property of the phrase, is a tone, and is not final when inherent-low syllables follow. T. Payne 1993 could not be opened (lending-only), so no statement from it is available.
